tasks.title: Listening 2 — Interview

items.stem: When did preparation begin?
How long did the team work?

tasks.transcript:
Interviewer: Welcome to our school identity programme. What encouraged you to make a personal photo board, Huda?
Huda: I noticed that classmates who seemed different often shared hobbies, so I wanted to help people discover them.
Interviewer: Did the first display focus only on people's appearance, or did you include their interests as well?
Huda: We included their hobbies, family traditions and personal strengths. Appearance cannot explain the whole story of someone's identity.
Interviewer: Where did your team first collect information for the project?
Huda: We visited three classes and offered simple questionnaires. Everyone was free to answer privately or leave a question blank.
Interviewer: When did you begin preparing the photographs?
Huda: We started in October and worked for nearly three weeks before the first display was ready.
Interviewer: Who helped you organise the captions, and which languages did you decide to use?
Huda: Our English teacher helped us. We wrote short captions in both Arabic and English so more families could understand.
Interviewer: Did you keep the photograph when one classmate changed her mind about showing it?
Huda: No. We removed her picture immediately and used a drawing instead. Respecting someone's choice matters more than a display.
Interviewer: How did the project change the way students talked to one another at school?
Huda: People began asking about interests rather than making quick assumptions. Several shy pupils also joined clubs that suited them.

tasks.title: Reading 2 — Short answers
tasks.passage:
When Aisha joined a new school in Sohar, she worried that her classmates would not understand her interests. She loved astronomy and usually spent Friday evenings looking at the night sky. Her desk partner, Salma, enjoyed art and was always drawing. At first, the girls had little to talk about. Then their teacher asked the class to organise a display about personal identity. Aisha suggested a simple model of the solar system while Salma offered to design the posters. They invited two other pupils: Hamad, who was confident speaking to visitors, and Noura, who preferred organising details quietly. The project succeeded because each student contributed a different strength. Aisha now believes identity is not only about appearance or nationality; it also includes values, habits, abilities and the way people treat one another. She still enjoys astronomy, but she is learning that sharing an interest can be easier when she listens to other people first.

The pupils prepared labels describing the main idea behind each part of the display. They checked the spelling of names and asked everyone for permission before sharing personal details. When visitors arrived, Salma introduced the posters and Aisha explained why the solar system model mattered to her. Some younger children had never used a telescope, so she described what they might see in the night sky. Afterwards, the group discussed what they had learned about friendship and confidence. They discovered that listening to a quiet classmate can reveal important skills. They also promised to welcome new pupils and avoid judging them without getting to know them first.

tasks.transcript:
Interviewer: Today we are discussing how young people can protect languages and share stories. Why did your class begin this project, Bilal?
Bilal: We realised that some children understood their grandparents' words but rarely tried speaking the same language themselves.
Interviewer: Were you studying only written words, or were you interested in conversations and stories as well?
Bilal: We focused on conversations. A language lives through the people who use it and tell stories in it.
Interviewer: Where did your first interview take place?
Bilal: We recorded our first interview at the community centre with my grandmother, who loves telling family stories.
Interviewer: What happened while you were checking the recording, and how did your team respond to the problem?
Bilal: The microphone stopped working for a few minutes. We checked the batteries and repeated that section patiently.
Interviewer: What language did the grandparents speak during the interview?
Bilal: They spoke Arabic, and two pupils added short English summaries so the whole class could learn from them.
Interviewer: When did you share the collection?
Bilal: We shared it on Tuesday during the school exhibition, but we used only recordings that families had approved.
Interviewer: What was the most important lesson you learned about communication through this project?
Bilal: Listening respectfully is as important as speaking clearly. We should ask questions instead of pretending we understand.

tasks.title: Reading 2 — Short answers
tasks.passage:
Last term, Mariam and her classmates were making a short film about communication in their town. They interviewed grandparents who remembered sharing news by letter, and younger people who used messaging apps every day. While they were editing the film, a recorded interview disappeared from the shared folder. Everyone thought the file had been deleted. Mariam was checking the computer when she noticed a message from Bilal. He explained that he had moved the recording to a different folder to protect it from accidental changes. Unfortunately, he had forgotten to tell the team. The students felt relieved, but they also realised that a useful action can cause confusion if nobody explains it. They agreed to keep a simple record whenever a file was moved and to listen carefully when someone raised a concern. The finished film showed more than changes in technology: it showed why clear messages, careful listening and trust matter in every generation.

Before presenting the film, the team prepared short English subtitles so younger viewers could follow unfamiliar expressions. They asked each interviewee for permission to share their story and removed personal details when necessary. A teacher checked the captions against the original recordings. During the screening, several visitors asked how people had stayed connected before mobile phones. Mariam explained that families often wrote letters or arranged meetings in advance. After the event, the pupils discussed the advantages and disadvantages of modern technology. Some thought instant messages were convenient, while others valued the time and care required to write a letter. They agreed that understanding depends on clear explanations, not just fast devices.

tasks.title: Listening 2 — Interview

items.stem: Who suggested the invention?
What activates the reminder?
Where will students test the prototype?
What problem was found in the early version?
When is the next meeting with the engineer?

tasks.transcript:
Interviewer: Welcome to Future Voices. What kind of technology is your science club developing, Noura?
Noura: We are building a simple device that reminds older people to drink water at regular times during the day.
Interviewer: Did the idea come from a famous inventor, or did someone in your local community suggest it?
Noura: My grandmother suggested it when she forgot to drink enough water during a busy afternoon last year.
Interviewer: How will the device work?
Noura: A timer activates a small light and a sound. It never gives medical advice; people still make their own decisions.
Interviewer: Where are the students going to test the prototype, and who is supervising the trial?
Noura: We are going to test it in the science laboratory next month with our teacher and a volunteer engineer.
Interviewer: What happened when you tried an early version, and how are you changing the design because of that problem?
Noura: The warning was too quiet, so we are adding a brighter signal as well as a clearer button.
Interviewer: When is your team meeting the engineer again?
Noura: We are meeting her on Wednesday. The school timetable confirms that she will arrive before the second break.
Interviewer: What advice would you give other students who want to design useful technology for families?
Noura: Ask people what they need, test your ideas carefully and remember that technology should support human judgement.

tasks.title: Reading 2 — Short answers
tasks.passage:
A group of students at a school in Nizwa is planning a small smart garden. The project will use sensors to measure moisture in the soil, and a simple app will display the results. The students are going to test the first prototype next month. Their science teacher reminds them that a sensor cannot make every decision. For example, the app may report dry soil, but the team must check whether a plant actually needs water before opening the irrigation system. Some pupils think artificial intelligence will make gardening easier; others worry that relying completely on technology could waste water when a sensor breaks. The group is meeting a local engineer on Tuesday to discuss those risks. A school exhibition opens at nine o'clock on Thursday, and the pupils hope to demonstrate the garden there. They will collect feedback and improve the design before producing a larger version. They want to show that useful inventions combine technology with responsible human judgement.

To make the system safer, students included a manual control that could stop watering whenever necessary. They tested the device in different conditions rather than trusting a single result. The engineer showed them how to record measurements and notice unusual readings. She also reminded them not to make promises about the invention until it had been checked properly. At the exhibition, families asked questions about saving water and protecting plants during hot weather. Some visitors wanted a brighter warning light, while others preferred a simpler display. The class wrote down these suggestions and decided to improve the prototype before using it on a larger garden.
